title: Follicles & Functional Cysts
front clue: Dominant follicle grows to about 2 cm, then becomes a crenulated corpus luteum
core concept: Each cycle several antral follicles develop in the ovary. By about days 8 to 12 one dominant follicle is selected and grows about 2 to 3 mm per day, reaching about 20 to 24 mm before ovulation; a cumulus oophorus may be seen as a small echogenic mural bump. After ovulation the follicle collapses, a small amount of free fluid may appear in the cul-de-sac, and the corpus luteum forms: a thick-walled, often crenulated cyst with low-level echoes and a peripheral ring of color flow. A follicle that fails to ovulate and keeps growing becomes a follicular cyst, usually defined as a simple cyst over about 3 cm. A hemorrhagic cyst shows a fine reticular, lacy or fishnet pattern, or a retracting clot with concave margins that has no internal color flow; it usually resolves within about 6 to 12 weeks. Per O-RADS US, simple cysts up to 3 cm in premenopausal women are normal physiologic findings, and typical hemorrhagic cysts under 5 cm need no follow-up.
why it matters: Most adnexal cysts in menstruating women are physiologic, so the exam rewards recognizing benign patterns rather than reflexively calling them masses. The key differentiators of a hemorrhagic cyst are a reticular pattern and an avascular clot; any internal flow points away from clot toward a solid component. A trap is mistaking a corpus luteum for an ectopic pregnancy; it is inside the ovary. Another is reporting a normal dominant follicle as a cyst. Hemorrhagic cysts change over time, so follow-up after menses distinguishes them from endometriomas.
on the registry: Questions ask for the size of a mature follicle, signs of ovulation, the appearance of hemorrhagic cysts and O-RADS management of physiologic cysts.
checkpoint: Hemorrhagic cyst: lacy pattern, retracting clot, no internal flow

title: Endometrioma & Dermoid
front clue: Ground glass and persistent: endometrioma; bright plug with shadowing: dermoid
core concept: An endometrioma is a cyst lined by endometrial tissue that fills with old blood. The classic appearance is a unilocular or few-loculated cyst with homogeneous low-level internal echoes (ground-glass), no internal vascularity, and sometimes small echogenic wall foci. They may be multiple or bilateral, are associated with pain, dysmenorrhea and infertility, and do not resolve over time like hemorrhagic cysts. Adhesions may pull both ovaries together behind the uterus (kissing ovaries). In pregnancy, decidualized endometriomas may show vascular solid-looking wall projections that can mimic malignancy. A mature cystic teratoma (dermoid) is the most common ovarian germ cell tumor. Signs include an echogenic mural nodule (Rokitansky nodule or dermoid plug), often with shadowing; the tip-of-the-iceberg sign, where an echogenic front surface shadows the rest; hyperechoic lines and dots from hair (dot-dash pattern); a fat-fluid level; and calcifications. Dermoids are bilateral in about 10 to 15 percent and increase the risk of torsion. Classic appearances of both lesions are scored O-RADS 2 when under 10 cm.
why it matters: These two lesions are classic benign patterns, and recognizing them avoids unnecessary concern. For endometrioma, the uniform low-level echoes and lack of flow are key, while a hemorrhagic cyst typically shows a lacy pattern and resolves. For dermoid, the trap is the tip-of-the-iceberg sign: shadowing hides the true size and can make the mass look like bowel gas, so a dermoid can be missed entirely. A dermoid is also a common reason for ovarian torsion. Any vascular solid component should prompt reconsideration.
on the registry: Expect sign-based items (ground glass, Rokitansky nodule, tip of the iceberg, dot-dash) and questions on clinical associations and follow-up behavior.
checkpoint: Endometrioma persists; hemorrhagic cyst resolves

title: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
front clue: Two of three: irregular cycles, androgen excess, polycystic ovarian morphology
core concept: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common endocrine disorder of women of reproductive age. Using the Rotterdam criteria, diagnosis requires two of three: oligo-ovulation or anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound, after other causes are excluded. Current international guidelines define polycystic morphology on a transvaginal scan with a high-frequency probe (about 8 MHz) as 20 or more follicles of 2 to 9 mm per ovary, and/or an ovarian volume of 10 mL or more, without a dominant follicle, corpus luteum or cyst. Ovarian volume is calculated as length times width times height times 0.523. The classic appearance is enlarged ovaries with many small peripheral follicles (string of pearls) and increased central echogenic stroma. Ultrasound is not recommended for diagnosing PCOS within about 8 years of menarche, because multifollicular ovaries are normal in adolescents. Clinical associations include obesity, insulin resistance and infertility. Chronic unopposed estrogen increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma, and PCOS patients are at higher risk of OHSS during ovulation induction.
why it matters: The exam wants you to know that ultrasound cannot diagnose PCOS alone; morphology is only one of three criteria, and many normal women have polycystic-appearing ovaries. A trap is applying adult follicle-count criteria to an adolescent. Another is counting with a low-frequency transabdominal probe, which undercounts follicles. The endometrium deserves attention too: anovulation means unopposed estrogen and potential hyperplasia. In fertility treatment, many small follicles mean an exaggerated response and a high risk of hyperstimulation.
on the registry: Questions ask for the Rotterdam criteria, the follicle number and volume thresholds, the ovarian volume formula and the endometrial risk.
checkpoint: 20 or more follicles, or 10 mL or more, per ovary

title: Ovarian Torsion
front clue: Big edematous ovary with peripheral follicles; normal flow does not exclude torsion
core concept: Ovarian torsion is twisting of the ovary, often with the fallopian tube, on its vascular pedicle, first obstructing venous and lymphatic outflow and then arterial inflow. It presents with sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain. It is most common in reproductive-age women and children, is more frequent on the right, and is often caused by an ovarian mass or cyst, classically a dermoid, larger than about 5 cm; pregnancy and ovulation induction with enlarged ovaries increase the risk. The most consistent finding is a unilaterally enlarged ovary compared with the other side. Other signs include stromal edema with peripherally displaced follicles (string of pearls), an abnormal midline or high position, free fluid and a twisted vascular pedicle (whirlpool sign). Doppler may show decreased or absent venous and arterial flow, but normal arterial flow does not exclude torsion, because the ovary has a dual supply from the ovarian artery and the adnexal branch of the uterine artery and torsion may be partial or intermittent. Torsion is a surgical emergency.
why it matters: This is a classic exam trap: the presence of Doppler flow does not rule out torsion. The size asymmetry and clinical picture matter more than color flow, because venous obstruction comes first and arterial flow may persist. A twisted pedicle is the most specific sign when seen. Another trap is assuming torsion needs a mass; normal ovaries can twist, especially in children. Compare both ovaries and look for a lead mass such as a dermoid or a large cyst.
on the registry: Expect pain scenarios asking for the most consistent sign, the significance of preserved Doppler flow, and the typical predisposing mass.
checkpoint: Flow present does not mean torsion absent

title: O-RADS & Ovarian Neoplasms
front clue: Solid tissue with strong flow, papillary projections, ascites: high risk
core concept: O-RADS US sorts adnexal lesions into risk categories: 0 incomplete, 1 normal premenopausal ovary, 2 almost certainly benign (under 1 percent risk), 3 low risk (1 to under 10 percent), 4 intermediate (10 to under 50 percent) and 5 high risk (50 percent or more). Features that raise concern are solid components, especially irregular ones, papillary projections (solid tissue at least 3 mm tall protruding into a cyst), thick irregular septations, color score 3 or 4 flow in solid tissue, and ascites or peritoneal nodules, which place a lesion in O-RADS 5. Epithelial tumors are most common: serous cystadenomas are usually unilocular, while serous cystadenocarcinoma is the most common ovarian malignancy, often bilateral with papillary projections. Mucinous tumors tend to be large and multiloculated with locules of different echogenicity. Fibroma and fibrothecoma are solid, hypoechoic, shadowing masses and may cause Meigs syndrome (ascites and pleural effusion). Granulosa cell tumors produce estrogen and can thicken the endometrium. Krukenberg tumors are bilateral metastases.
why it matters: Think of O-RADS as feature recognition rather than memorizing histology: the more solid, irregular and vascular a lesion is, the higher the category. A trap is overcalling avascular contents, such as clot in a hemorrhagic cyst or a dermoid plug, as solid tissue; lack of flow and classic patterns help. Another is ignoring the rest of the abdomen, since ascites and peritoneal implants upgrade risk. Solid hypoechoic shadowing masses are often benign fibromas, while estrogen effects on the endometrium suggest a granulosa cell tumor.
on the registry: Questions describe a lesion in words and ask for the O-RADS category or the most concerning feature, and match tumor types with their syndromes.
checkpoint: More solid, more vascular, more fluid in the belly: more risk

title: Hydrosalpinx, PID & TOA
front clue: Tubular fluid with incomplete septa; a tender complex mass with fever is TOA
core concept: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is an ascending infection, most often from chlamydia or gonorrhea, that progresses from the cervix to the endometrium, tubes, ovaries and peritoneum. Early PID may show a normal scan. Findings include endometrial thickening or fluid (endometritis), free fluid with debris, thick-walled, fluid-filled tubes. A pyosalpinx is a distended tube filled with echogenic fluid with a thick, hyperemic wall. The cogwheel sign, thickened endosalpingeal folds seen in cross section, indicates acute inflammation. A tubo-ovarian complex is inflamed tube and ovary that can still be told apart; a tubo-ovarian abscess (TOA) is a complex, multilocular, thick-walled mass in which the ovary can no longer be identified, often with hyperemia and fluid-debris levels. Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome is perihepatic inflammation causing right upper quadrant pain. A hydrosalpinx is a chronic, fluid-filled, tubular C or S-shaped structure separate from the ovary, with incomplete septations (folds) and a waist sign; the beads-on-a-string sign of small mural nodules indicates chronic disease. Hydrosalpinx lowers IVF success, so salpingectomy may be advised.
why it matters: The tube is identified by shape: incomplete septations and a waist distinguish a dilated tube from a multilocular ovarian cyst, which has complete septations. A trap is calling a hydrosalpinx an ovarian cyst and following it unnecessarily; scan along the structure to show it is tubular. Acute versus chronic depends on wall thickness and folds: cogwheel is acute, beads on a string is chronic. TOA versus tubo-ovarian complex depends on whether the ovary can still be seen. Clinical findings, fever and tenderness, frame the diagnosis.
on the registry: Expect scenarios with fever and pelvic pain, signs of acute versus chronic tubal disease, and the difference between tubo-ovarian complex and abscess.
checkpoint: Cogwheel is acute; beads on a string is chronic

title: Ovulation Induction & OHSS
front clue: Measure follicles, trigger near 18 to 20 mm, watch for huge ovaries and ascites
core concept: Ovulation induction uses drugs such as letrozole, clomiphene or injectable gonadotropins. A baseline transvaginal scan early in the cycle (about day 2 or 3) checks for residual cysts and records the antral follicle count (follicles about 2 to 10 mm). Serial scans measure each growing follicle and record endometrial thickness and pattern. An hCG or GnRH-agonist trigger is usually given when lead follicles reach about 18 to 20 mm for timed intercourse or insemination, or when several follicles reach about 17 to 18 mm in IVF. A trilaminar endometrium of about 7 mm or more is favorable. Too many mature follicles may lead to cycle cancellation to prevent multiple pregnancy and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS). OHSS usually follows the trigger or early pregnancy, which raises hCG. It produces enlarged ovaries, often 5 to 10 cm or more, filled with many large cysts (spoke-wheel appearance), plus ascites, pleural effusion, hemoconcentration, oliguria and thrombosis risk. Risk factors include PCOS, young age, high antral follicle count and high estradiol. Enlarged ovaries can torse.
why it matters: Monitoring is about balance: enough follicles to achieve pregnancy, not so many that the patient risks multiples or OHSS. Exams ask what to measure (follicle size and count, endometrium), when to trigger, and what OHSS looks like. A trap is misreading the large stimulated cysts as malignant multilocular masses; the history is decisive. Remember the fluid shifts: scan the abdomen and chest for ascites and effusions. Pregnancy prolongs OHSS because hCG keeps stimulating the ovaries, and heterotopic pregnancy risk is higher in these patients.
on the registry: Questions ask for the trigger follicle size, the antral follicle count definition, OHSS findings and risk factors, and which complications to scan for.
checkpoint: Spoke-wheel ovaries plus ascites after a trigger means OHSS

title: Sonohysterography
front clue: Early proliferative phase, saline through a catheter, no pregnancy and no infection
core concept: Saline infusion sonohysterography (SIS) distends the endometrial cavity with sterile saline introduced through a thin catheter during transvaginal imaging, outlining the endometrium. Indications include abnormal uterine bleeding, a thickened or poorly seen endometrium, suspected polyps or submucosal fibroids, infertility, suspected adhesions, and evaluation of congenital anomalies. It is ideally performed in the early proliferative phase, after menstrual bleeding stops and before ovulation, about days 5 to 10, when the endometrium is thinnest and an early pregnancy is not at risk. Contraindications include pregnancy and active pelvic infection or PID; unexplained pelvic tenderness should also delay the study. Flush the catheter with saline beforehand, because air bubbles can mimic polyps. A polyp appears as an echogenic intracavitary mass covered by endometrium, a submucosal fibroid as a hypoechoic broad-based mass beneath the endometrium, hyperplasia as diffuse thickening, and adhesions (Asherman syndrome) as echogenic bands bridging the cavity. A balloon catheter in the lower segment can hide lesions there, so deflate it at the end. Agitated saline can assess tubal patency (sonosalpingography).
why it matters: Timing and contraindications are the most tested points. Scheduling in the early proliferative phase avoids disrupting a possible early pregnancy and gives the thinnest lining, so small polyps stand out. A trap is calling air bubbles polyps; bubbles are very bright, may shadow and move. Another is mistaking blood clot for a lesion; clot moves and lacks flow. Always look at the lower segment and cervix after deflating the balloon, because the balloon itself can hide lesions there.
on the registry: Expect questions on timing in the cycle, contraindications, artifacts from air, and the appearance of polyps, fibroids and adhesions.
checkpoint: Days 5 to 10, flush the air, check below the balloon

title: Amniocentesis & CVS
front clue: Amnio from 15 weeks in a cord-free pocket; CVS at 10 to 13 weeks
core concept: Amniocentesis samples amniotic fluid under continuous ultrasound guidance, usually from 15 weeks onward. Before the procedure, confirm fetal cardiac activity, gestational age, number of fetuses, placental location and a suitable pocket. Choose a pocket free of cord and fetal parts, ideally avoiding the placenta, and keep the needle tip in view. Early amniocentesis before 15 weeks increases pregnancy loss and clubfoot and is avoided. The procedure-related loss rate is low, often quoted at about 0.1 to 0.3 percent. Amniotic fluid can be tested for karyotype and microarray, infection and AFP with acetylcholinesterase for open neural tube defects. Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) obtains placental villi at about 10 to 13 weeks by a transcervical or transabdominal route, targeting the chorion frondosum. CVS before about 10 weeks is linked with limb reduction defects; confined placental mosaicism, in about 1 to 2 percent, may require amniocentesis to clarify; and CVS cannot assess AFP. After either procedure, document fetal heart activity, and give Rh-negative unsensitized patients Rh immune globulin.
why it matters: Remember what each test samples: amniocentesis samples fetal cells and fluid, while CVS samples placenta, which explains mosaicism and the absence of AFP testing with CVS. The sonographer's role is planning and guidance: choose the pocket, track the needle tip, and confirm heart activity before and after. A trap is choosing the largest pocket even when the cord lies within it; color Doppler should confirm no cord in the path. Remember the Rh immune globulin step for Rh-negative patients.
on the registry: Questions ask for the timing of each procedure, why early amniocentesis is avoided, what CVS cannot test, and the sonographer's steps before and after.
checkpoint: CVS samples placenta, amnio samples fluid

title: Safety, ALARA & Transvaginal Technique
front clue: Lowest output, shortest time, TIS early and TIB later, a clean covered probe
core concept: No confirmed harmful bioeffects of diagnostic ultrasound have been shown in the human fetus, but ultrasound deposits energy, so the ALARA principle (as low as reasonably achievable) applies: scan only when medically indicated, use the lowest output and shortest time that answers the question, and prefer receiver gain over transmit power. Monitor the on-screen thermal index (TI), the estimate of tissue heating, and mechanical index (MI), the estimate of cavitation risk. In the first trimester, before significant bone ossification, the soft tissue thermal index (TIS) is used; from about 10 weeks, when fetal bone is present, the bone thermal index (TIB) is more relevant. Spectral and color Doppler produce higher exposure than gray-scale imaging, so in early pregnancy cardiac activity is documented with M-mode. Transvaginal scanning requires an empty bladder, an explanation of the exam and consent, a chaperone according to policy, a probe cover (non-latex for latex allergy) and high-level disinfection between patients. A full bladder helps transabdominal pelvic imaging by displacing bowel.
why it matters: The exam tests which index applies when and the practical steps of ALARA. Raising receiver gain improves brightness without increasing exposure, so it is the first choice; increasing output power is not. Doppler on an embryo is the classic wrong answer for documenting heart rate. For transvaginal scanning, the most tested points are bladder status, probe cover and high-level disinfection, since a probe cover can tear. A trap is filling the bladder before a transvaginal scan; it pushes the pelvic organs out of the near field.
on the registry: Expect questions on the meaning of TI and MI, which TI to use by gestational age, how to apply ALARA, and the preparation and disinfection of transvaginal probes.
checkpoint: Gain before power; M-mode before Doppler
